The two arrows meeting head to head at success, all in the accent color, form a collider: two causes with a common effect. The card returns the one collider as the triple (talent, success, luck), effect in the middle." width="100%"} A collider is a triple `(p1, c, p2)` with edges `p1 -> c` and `p2 -> c`: two causes with a common effect. In causal diagrams colliders behave specially, since conditioning on a collider (or one of its descendants) *creates* a dependence between its causes (see `is_d_separator()`), the source of selection bias such as Berkson's paradox. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Every collider `(p1, c, p2)` as node IDs, one per unordered pair of parents of each node. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Every pair of distinct in-neighbors of every node, $O(\sum_v \deg^-(v)^2)$. Matches NetworkX's `dag.colliders` (and the deprecated `compute_v_structures`). ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#ed279ea7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["talent", "luck", "success"]) g.add_edges([("talent", "success"), ("luck", "success")]) [tuple(g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in triple) for triple in g.colliders()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('talent', 'success', 'luck')] ``` ::: :::
